segments.description: Hello everyone, my name is Jose Canos and I come from Castellón, Spain. I am a strength and conditioning coach and I have spent all my career helping tennis players, not only to get stronger but also stay healthy and have longer careers. In my presentation I will talk about one of the most common and frustrating challenges in our sports, shoulders injuries, which remain one of the worst enemies a tennis players can face. I would like to thank Tennis Australia for this opportunity. It is a great honour for me to be one of the speakers at this virtual coaches conference. Let us start with the reality of tennis as a sport. Tennis is beautiful but is a highly asymmetrical sport. Every forehand, every serve and every overhead places repetitive stress in one side of the body, repeating the same motion thousands of times every week. This leads to muscular imbalances, especially between the internal and external rotators of the shoulder and between the anterior and posterior stabilisers of the scapula. Over time, these imbalances create what I like to call the hidden enemy of the tennis shoulder. Tennis and overdevelopment of pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi, internal rotators, weakness and inhibition of infraspinators and t-dice minors, external rotators. A loss offers scapular control, especially from the serratus anterior and lower tapissius. This changes not only increase the risk of shoulder impingement and rotator calf injuries

but also reduce performance, because a dysfunctional shoulder cannot produce efficient power. Before we move into the practical phases of preventive work, let's take a brief look at what current scientific research tells us about shoulder injuries in tennis. A recent study called shoulder injuries in tennis players concludes by saying that. To reduce the risk of shoulder injury in tennis, carefully evaluation of kinetic chain function, scapular function, rotator calf muscles balance and the integrity of the capsular structures should be carried out. And specific training programs incorporating scapular stabilization and capsular stretching at the early stage of shoulder injury can prevent intraarticular damage of the shoulder. Another article shows that the domino shoulder internal rotation and total range of motion were significantly decreased during the three hours tennis match. This alteration in shoulder roam had the potential to increase shoulder injury risk and negatively influence serve performance during match play. Consequently, tennis players are encouraged to restore the normal shoulder internal and total roam through stretching and recovery techniques. A further study highlights that shoulder-overused injuries are more prevalent among competitors over head-john athletes. Coaches working with older and more experienced young players, especially those training more than 11 hours per week, should be aware of increased risk of shoulder and elbow-overused

injuries. Finally, a systematic review published in 2020 concludes that problem tennis play, scapular disc kinesis, muscle fatigue, scapular thoracic properties, shoulder kinetics and kinematics, skill level and technique were all identified as risk factors for upper-leaning injury in tennis players. Identified risk factors can help clinicians, sports scientists and coaches design more effective injury prevention strategies and ultimately enhance player performance. Now, the key message I want to emphasize today is this. Prevention and rehabilitation are not the same thing. What I'm going to present is not for players who are already injured, but for healthy athletes who want to stay healthy throughout their careers. Preventive training must be a daily habit, not a temporary fix. Just as a player trains the forehand or serve, they must also train their shoulder stability and scapular control. This kind of work is the invisible foundation that allows everything else, technique, endurance, strength to function safely. To structure this concept, I propose a simple and practical model consisting of five phases. Each phase has a specific goal and targets, a different component of shoulder health. In the first phase, we focus on myofascial release, using foam rollers or massage balls to work on the shot tissue. The main objective here is to realize accumulated tension in overall muscles and improve the

overall quality of the tissue. This allows the shoulder to move more freely and naturally. Our focus is on key areas that tend to become tight, intense players. The pectoral is major, latissimus dorsi and the posterior shoulder, helping to reduce the restriction that limit both mobility and performance. Because, as I like to say, a healthy shoulder starts with quality tissue. Before we build strength, we must first create freedom of movement. In the second phase, we move into mobility work. The main objective here is to increase the range of motion of shoulder joint and to improve thoracic and scapular mobility, both essential for efficient and pain-free shoulder mechanics. The focus is on creating balanced movement between the glenohumeral joint and the scapular through dynamic mobility and stretching exercises. This helps the shoulder move smoothly through all the positions required in tennis, from the serve to the forehand follow-through. As I like to remind my players, mobility is the bridge between flexibility and control. It gives the shoulder the space it needs to move efficiently and pain-free. In this phase, our goal is to re-educate the neuro-muscular system so that the stabilizing muscles activate correctly and shoulder coordination improves. We focus on key stabilizers, such as the radius interior, the lower tapetures and the stern rotators. These muscles are essential for proper scapular control and joint alignment, which are the

foundation for safe and efficient movement. Remember this, strength without control is wasted potential. Motor control ensures that every muscle fires at the right time, in the right way. In this phase, we focus on developing balanced strength and integrating shoulder stability into dynamic sport-specific movements. The goal is to reinforce the rotator cuff, scapular retactors and posterior chain, while connecting upper body strength with core engagement to generate tennis-specific power. This is the turning point, where strength meets control to save work, your shoulder. Without inter-reparation, power becomes a risk. Here, we build the foundation to performance and long-term success in tennis, and support active recovery between sessions. We focus on gentle stretching, breathing control and soft tissue, release to restore, balance and prepare the shoulder for the next training load. Remember this, strength without control is wasted potential. Motor control ensures that every muscle fires at the right time, in the right way. Recovery is your secret weapon, by prioritizing flexibility and active recovery, we protect the shoulder, prevent injuries and ensure it is very strong and mobile for every match ahead. How do we turn this concept into action? Injury prevention for tennis players should not be an occasional fix. It must become a daily habit. Why? Because tennis is an asymmetrical sport, highly demanding and prone to create muscular imbalances.

These imbalances, if ignored, lead to pain, injuries and shortened careers. By integrating preventive work into the player's routine, we preserve physical health, reduce this comfort and ultimately extend their careers while posting performance. A complete preventive session can take just 30 to 40 minutes, easily adapted to any training schedule, but even 5 to 10 minutes of target scapular activation before stepping on court can make a significant difference in shoulder health and efficiency. The goal is not fatigue, it is quality of movement. Every repetition should reinforce stability, control and balance. This is the invisible work that keeps players free, powerful and ready for the demands of the game. To conclude, I want to leave you with this thought. The shoulder is not just a joint, it's a system and like any system, it needs maintenance. If we as a coach and professionals can teach players to value preventive work as much as technical work, we will extend their careers, enhance their performance and reduce one of the most common sources of frustration in tennis, shoulder injuries. Thank you very much for your attention and for your shared patience for keeping our athletes healthy and strong.
